title: Curios of the Week #169
author: Greg Ashman
summary: This AI special edition of Greg Ashman's weekly curios roundup opens with two 'bad ideas of the week' concerning AI and assessment. The first targets the Australian Government Primary Principals Association's proposal to abolish NAPLAN writing assessments and replace them with tasks that allow students to use AI to draft, edit, and refine writing while being assessed on 'creativity and critical thinking.' Ashman's critique is pointed: this is the same logic as allowing calculators before students have learned arithmetic, and it rests on the fundamentally misguided view that education is purely functional preparation for work, where any tool that can substitute for human effort should simply be adopted. The second bad idea involves academics who are developing similarly permissive AI-in-assessment frameworks. The roundup also covers an episode of Ashman's When Will They Learn? podcast discussing critiques of cognitive load theory and EEF findings on ability grouping. This edition functions as a curated editorial commentary on the most contested current questions in AI and education policy.
points: * The AGPPA's proposal to allow students to use AI to draft writing in assessments represents -- in Ashman's view -- a fundamental category error: the purpose of teaching writing is not to produce written documents but to develop the human capacity to write; removing the productive struggle removes the learning. * Ashman draws the parallel explicitly: 'This is exactly like suggesting students should never have to solve arithmetic problems by hand because calculators exist, that they should never learn to draw because cameras exist.' The argument is not that tools are bad but that tools cannot substitute for the skill-building process that precedes tool-augmented performance. * The critique of the 'education is purely functional preparation for work' view is sharp: if the goal of education is only to produce workers who can use available tools, then any human skill that a tool can replicate is automatically obsolete in the curriculum -- an impoverished and ultimately self-defeating vision. * A further practical objection: students who never learn to write themselves will never be able to 'filter, sort, or improve upon the bland regurgitations of ChatGPT' -- the capacity to evaluate and improve AI output depends on the human capability that assessment-via-AI proposals would eliminate. * The roundup also covers Ashman's podcast episode (When Will They Learn? #9) discussing critiques of cognitive load theory and EEF ability grouping findings, signaling ongoing engagement with the contested empirical foundations of evidence-based teaching.
quotes: This week's Curios is an artificial intelligence special edition.

[AGPPA President Pat Murphy] said any review needs to look at how to involve enhanced use of adaptive online testing, shorter targeted assessments, and tasks that measure critical thinking, problem-solving, communication, and digital literacy. Murphy said this could look like students drafting, editing, and refining writing using digital and AI tools while being assessed on creativity and critical thinking.

It is hard to find the words to condemn such an idea. We are here to teach students how to write. Learning to write is of value in its own right. If students later choose to use AI -- with caution -- in a professional context, then that is up to them. First, however, we should teach them how to write.

This is exactly like suggesting students should never have to solve arithmetic problems by hand because calculators exist, that they should never learn to draw because cameras exist and that they should never learn to make music because AI music generators like Suno exist.

It results from the fundamental misunderstanding that education is a purely functional preparation for work and therefore, if tools are available to do tasks that once were done by hand, we should teach students to use those tools. Not only is this an impoverished, bleak and oddly capitalistic approach to education, it will not work in its own right. If students never learn to write themselves, then they will never be able to filter, sort, or improve upon the bland regurgitations of ChatGPT.
